claims.text: Rapid heating–quenching cycles induce formation of a stable nanoscale passive oxide film on high-entropy alloys.
The induced passive oxide film simultaneously improves mechanical-wear and corrosion resistance.
Rapid heating–quenching produces or maintains a refined, self-healing surface microstructure.
The initial high-entropy alloy is a metastable, multielement solid solution.
The treated surface contains a refined quasi-amorphous or nanocrystalline microstructure in addition to the nanoscale passive film.
Rapid thermal cycling locks in a distinctive HEA microstructure that favors formation of a uniform passive oxide layer.
The passive oxide layer is self-repairing and rapidly reforms at sites damaged by wear.
Rapid film reformation reduces exposure of electrochemically active corrosion sites during wear.
Reduced exposure of active sites mitigates synergistic mechanical and chemical degradation.
The thermally treated HEA will have a lower wear rate than the duplex stainless-steel baseline under matched tribocorrosion conditions.
The thermally treated HEA will have a lower corrosion-current density than the duplex stainless-steel baseline.
The treated HEA's combined tribocorrosion degradation will be less severe than the sum of wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
The predicted advantage should hold under controlled rapid heating–quenching and moderate mechanical loads.
Excessively high mechanical loads may eliminate the treated HEA's advantage.
Insufficient thermal cycling may fail to lock in the desired microstructure and eliminate the predicted advantage.
The magnitude of the wear and corrosion reductions depends on alloy composition and thermal-cycling parameters.
